facts.statement: Aymberedactylus is a genus of tapejarid pterosaur found in the Early Cretaceous Crato Formation of Brazil.
facts.quote: Aymberedactylus (meaning "small lizard finger") is a genus of tapejarid pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous Crato Formation of Brazil.

facts.statement: Aymberedactylus was discovered in the Aptian-Albian Crato Formation and described in 2016.
facts.quote: It was discovered in the Aptian-Albian Crato Formation, a konservat-lagerstätte well known for its exquisite preservation of fossils, and it was described in 2016.

facts.statement: The genus name Aymberedactylus comes from the Tupi word for "small lizard" and the Greek word for "finger," while the species name refers to the Brazilian state of Ceará.
facts.quote: The name Aymberedactylus is derived from the Tupi word aymbere ("small lizard") and Greek ("finger"), and the specific name refers to the Brazilian state of Ceará, which it was discovered in.

facts.statement: Aymberedactylus is identified by its toothless jaw, a dentary symphysis making up half the jaw length, and a small crest on the lower jaw.
facts.quote: Aymberedactylus can be identified as a tapejarine tapejarid from the holotypic jawbone due to its toothlessness, slightly downturned dentary symphysis which accounts for half of the total length of the jaw, and a small crest on the bottom of the dentary (which was incompletely preserved).

facts.statement: Small neurovascular foramina on the jaw suggest Aymberedactylus likely had a horned sheath over the tip of its jaw.
facts.quote: Small neurovascular foramina on the symphysis indicates the likely presence of a horned sheath over the tip of the jaw, which is also seen in Tupandactylus.

facts.statement: The preserved portion of the holotype mandible is 270 mm long.
facts.quote: The preserved portion is 270 mm long.

facts.statement: Aymberedactylus is distinguished by a long retroarticular process indicating good jaw control and a small depression with roughened bone texture on the splenial bone.
facts.quote: It can be distinguished from other pterosaurs by a long retroarticular process (a process to which the depressor mandibulae muscle attaches, implying that Aymberedactylus had good control over the movement of its jaw bones) and a small fossa, or depression, with a roughened bone texture on the splenial bone.

facts.statement: Aymberedactylus has a unique combination of traits including a deep shelf on the jaw symphysis, a wide jaw, and a short, shallow dentary fossa indicating a relatively weak bite.
facts.quote: In addition, Aymberedactylus shows a unique combination of traits: the shelf on the dentary symphysis is deep, the dorsal rim of the symphysis is concave, the jaw is relatively wide, the dentary fossa is short and shallow (which indicates a relatively weak bite), and the mandibular rami form a very large angle with the symphysis.

facts.statement: The preserved specimen of Aymberedactylus is estimated to have had a wingspan of approximately 2 meters.
facts.quote: The preserved specimen of Aymberedactylus would have had a wingspan of approximately 2 m, typical of tapejarids.

facts.statement: Because the skull bones were not fully fused, the preserved specimen of Aymberedactylus was likely a subadult.
facts.quote: Judging by how the bones in its skull were not yet entirely fused, it was likely a subadult.

facts.statement: A 2016 phylogenetic analysis recovered Aymberedactylus as the most basal tapejarine.
facts.quote: A phylogenetic analysis conducted in 2016 recovered Aymberedactylus as the most basal tapejarine.

facts.statement: Aymberedactylus lived during the Early Cretaceous, approximately 108 million years ago, in what is now South America.
facts.quote: Aymberedactylus (nombre que significa "dedo de pequeño lagarto de Ceará") es un género extinto de pterosaurio tapejárido vivió durante Cretácico Inferior, hace aproximadamente 108 millones de años cuyos restos se encontraron en la Formación Crato en Brasil en lo que hoy es Sudamérica.

facts.statement: Aymberedactylus lived between 119.57 and 113.2 million years ago during the Aptian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Aptian (119.57 to 113.2 million years ago)
